stem: Pipe A can fill a tank in 6 hours and pipe B can fill it in 12 hours. If both pipes are opened together on the empty tank, how long will they take to fill it?
explanation: Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/12 = 2/12 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 of the tank per hour. So the tank fills in 4 hours.

stem: An inlet pipe can fill an overhead tank in 10 hours and an outlet pipe can empty the full tank in 15 hours. If both are opened when the tank is empty, how long will it take to fill the tank?
explanation: Net filling rate = 1/10 − 1/15 = 3/30 − 2/30 = 1/30 of the tank per hour. So the tank fills in 30 hours.

stem: A pipe can fill a tank in 8 hours. Because of a leak at the bottom, the tank takes 2 hours longer to fill. If the tank is full, how long will the leak alone take to empty it?
explanation: With the leak the tank fills in 8 + 2 = 10 hours. Leak rate = 1/8 − 1/10 = 5/40 − 4/40 = 1/40 of the tank per hour, so the leak alone empties a full tank in 40 hours.

stem: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 15 hours respectively, while pipe C can empty the full tank in 20 hours. All three pipes are opened at 8:00 am on an empty tank. At what time will the tank be full?
explanation: Net rate = 1/12 + 1/15 − 1/20 = (5 + 4 − 3)/60 = 6/60 = 1/10 of the tank per hour. The tank fills in 10 hours, so it is full at 8:00 am + 10 h = 6:00 pm.
shortcut: Take tank = 60 units: A +5, B +4, C −3 → 6 units/hour → 10 hours

stem: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 20 minutes and 30 minutes respectively. Both are opened together on an empty tank, but after some time pipe B is closed and the tank gets filled in 15 minutes in all. After how many minutes was pipe B closed?
explanation: Pipe A runs for all 15 minutes and fills 15/20 = 3/4 of the tank. Pipe B must have filled the remaining 1/4, so B ran for 1/4 × 30 = 7.5 minutes. Check: 7.5 × (1/20 + 1/30) + 7.5 × 1/20 = 5/8 + 3/8 = 1.
shortcut: Credit the pipe that runs throughout first; the other fills the rest
